{#llpc} # Discussion

{#bsf2} Our study investigated the outcomes of lung cancer surgery in elderly patients, focusing on postoperative complications and mortality rates. We observed an in-hospital mortality rate of 1.7% after lung cancer surgery. Benker et al. [@w:w6] reported an overall operative mortality rate of 1.56%, similar to our finding. In contrast, Detillon et al. [@w:w7] found a higher operative mortality rate by 2.1% in patients ≥ 60 years with lung cancer resections compared to our data.

{#rv6g} ## Postoperative complications

{#za4h} We found that 28.9% of patients experienced postoperative pulmonary complications and 12.6% experienced cardiac complications classified as Clavien–Dindo grade ≥ II. These rates are higher compared to the previous studies reporting 10–15.4% for pulmonary complications in elderly patients undergoing lung resection [@w:w8]. Similary, Calado et al. [@w:w9] reported lower cardiac complications rates (8.2%) compared to our findings. In contrast, Srisomboon et al. [@w:w10] reported higher rate of respiratory (25%) and lower rates of cardiac complications (6%) in elderly patients undergoing thoracoscopic surgery.

{#qn4a} # Introduction

{#mfgo} Lung cancer is the most frequently occurring cancer and the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide . Pulmonary resection is key treatment for lung cancer but is often accompanied by significant postoperative complications, which may prolong hospital stay and incur greater medical expenses [@w:w1]. Surgical approaches for lung cancer, including video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) and thoracotomy, offer distinct advantages and challenges. Previous studies [@w:w2] suggest that VATS is superior to thoracotomy due to fewer postoperative complications.

{#elys} Patients undergoing thoracic surgery were more likely to be older. Poor physiological changes are common in elderly patients with complex comorbidities, which could complicate major noncardiac surgery, especially thoracic surgery, and negatively impact outcomes [@w:w3]. The risk of cardiopulmonary complications increases with age [@w:w4] and the incidence, characteristics, and risk factors of postoperative cardiopulmonary complications in noncardiac surgery in elderly patients could be different from those in the general population. It is imperative to evaluate better risk indicators to improve preoperative cardiac risk prediction in elderly patients.

{#aj9a} ## Factors associated with postoperative complications

{#t1df} The overall postoperative pulmonary and cardiac complications of Clavien–Dindo grade ≥ II were associated with age, male sex, body height, COPD, lower preoperative PFTs (% pre-operative FEV<sub>1</sub>, FEF<sub>25-75%</sub>, FEV<sub>1</sub>/FVC, % predicted FEV<sub>1</sub>), lobectomy, pneumonectomy, surgical time, intraoperative blood loss, and conversion from VATS to open thoracotomy. Age, coexistence of COPD, smoking, pneumonectomy, and conversion from VATS to open thoracotomy were significant predictors in the multivariable logistic model.

{#otaz} We found that patients aged ≥70 years were more likely to experience postoperative complications (Clavien-Dindo classification ≥2) in the univariate analysis. However, this association was attenuated in the multivariable model, suggesting that age alone may not be an independent predictor of postoperative complications. Similarly, previous studies have reported that patients aged ≥ 75 years did not exhibit increased surgical morbidity or mortality when appropriately selection for lung resection [@w:w11]. This suggests that age, while an important factor, may act as a surrogate for other predictors such as comorbidities (e.g., COPD) or intraoperative challenges.
